about: 📰 In the news: BibleChat matches a headline to the prophecy passages it touches, and shows how Christians read them. It gives no verdict and sets no dates. The news is chosen automatically twice a day from the sources below; each one is labelled.
caution_text: Watching, not counting: "of that day and hour knoweth no man" (Matthew 24:36), "Watch therefore" (Matthew 24:42), "Prove all things" (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Many have matched headlines to prophecy before and been wrong. Read the verses, and weigh the readings yourself.

readings.name: Futurist
readings.text: Most of Revelation and Daniel's last visions are still to come, and current events may be setting the stage.

readings.name: Historicist
readings.text: The visions unfold across church history, from the apostles to the return of Christ, with much already fulfilled.

readings.name: Preterist
readings.text: Much was fulfilled in the first century, above all in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70; the return of Christ is still to come.

readings.name: Idealist
readings.text: The visions picture the struggle between God and evil in every age, rather than one series of events.

themes.title: Israel and Jerusalem
themes.note: Many futurists see the return of the Jews to the land in 1948 and the place of Jerusalem today as signs of the end. Others read these promises as fulfilled in the return from Babylon, or in the church of Jew and Gentile together (Galatians 3:28-29), with Romans 11 still to come.

themes.title: Wars and rumours of wars
themes.note: Jesus said these things must come to pass, "but the end is not yet" (Matthew 24:6): wars mark the times, but do not date the end. Preterists read Matthew 24:6-8 as the years before AD 70; futurists and historicists as also pointing further ahead.

themes.title: Buying and selling: the mark of Revelation 13
themes.note: Some readers connect digital money, digital ID and implants with the mark. Others read the mark as a sign of loyalty, as God's servants are sealed in their foreheads (Revelation 7:3), not as a technology. The text ties the mark to worshipping the beast and his image.

themes.title: Famines, pestilences and earthquakes
themes.note: Jesus calls these "the beginning of sorrows" (Matthew 24:8), the first pains of birth, not the end itself. They have come in every century; Christians read them as reminders to be ready and to help those who suffer.

themes.title: Knowledge increased, and deception
themes.note: Some read Daniel 12:4 as the growth of travel and knowledge in our time; others as many people searching the sealed book to understand it. Jesus' first warning in Matthew 24 was "Take heed that no man deceive you" (Matthew 24:4).

themes.title: "Peace and safety": treaties and world powers
themes.note: Futurists often watch for a treaty involving Israel (Daniel 9:27) and a ten-king power (Revelation 17:12). Historicists and preterists read these verses as fulfilled in history, and many read Daniel 9:27 of Christ Himself, whose death ended the sacrifices.

themes.title: Persecution and the falling away
themes.note: Paul says the falling away comes before the day of Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Christians differ on whether it is one future event or a pattern seen in every age; 2 Timothy 3:5 tells Timothy to turn away from such people in his own day.

themes.title: The gospel to all nations
themes.note: Jesus linked the end to the gospel preached "in all the world for a witness unto all nations" (Matthew 24:14). Some count the languages still without a Bible; others note that Paul already spoke of the gospel going into all the world (Colossians 1:6).

themes.title: Signs in the sun, moon and stars
themes.note: Peter quoted Joel at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-20), so some read these signs as begun then; others watch for them in the sky before the Lord returns. Eclipses and comets come on schedules astronomers predict years ahead.

themes.title: Gog and Magog: Ezekiel 38
themes.note: Many futurists identify Rosh, Meshech and Persia with Russia and Iran and watch for an alliance against Israel. Others read Gog as a picture of all nations gathered against God's people, as Revelation 20:8 uses the names after the thousand years.

themes.title: Babylon: merchants and markets
themes.note: Interpreters identify Babylon as Rome (ancient or later), a future world system, or every proud power that trusts in riches. In Revelation 18 the merchants weep because "no man buyeth their merchandise any more" (Revelation 18:11).
